policeViolence: Told by a guy who has been on both sides of the shield — and has the bruises and the coffee stains to prove it Don't Hit Grandma With A Sign: How We Stop Police Violence Against Peaceful Manifestations A story in 12 chapters. Funny where it hurts, serious where it counts. If you are a protester, a cop, a mayor, or just someone who pays taxes for helmets to be banged against placards — this is for you. 1. The Square Where Nothing Dangerous Happened (Until The Vans Arrived) Let me tell you how it started, because I was there, with bad shoes and a borrowed sign. Tuesday, 6pm, Republic Square. Or Liberty Square. Honestly every city has the same square — pigeons, a closed kiosk, a statue of a guy on a horse who nobody can name. There were maybe 300 of us. Nurses asking for overtime pay. A couple teachers. Students with too much eyeliner and too little sleep. Dona Lurdes with her cookies. A kid with a drum who could not keep rhythm to save his life. Signs like “WE CAN’T BREATHE ON THESE WAGES” and “MY GRANDMA MARCHES FASTER THAN REFORM.” Dangerous stuff. Extremely dangerous cardboard. We chanted. Badly. Someone started “The people united” and half forgot the words and mumbled. A dog slept through it. A street vendor sold water at double price — capitalism survived the protest just fine. Then you heard them. Not chanting. Engines. Three vans, doors sliding like in movies. Shields, helmets, boots that cost more than my month’s rent. They lined up like we were an invading army. I swear the pigeons were more threatening that day — one actually stole a cop’s sandwich later, true story. Nothing had been broken. Nothing thrown. The only thing in the air was sweat and cheap sunscreen. But the line advanced. And that’s the first lesson I want tattooed on every city hall wall: peace does not break by itself. Someone has to come break it. I’m not an AI writing from a cloud. I’m a man who carried his neighbor’s kid on his shoulders that day because the kid wanted to see. I remember the smell of popcorn from the corner. I remember thinking: if anyone hits anyone here, it won’t be us starting it. We didn’t even have sticks for the signs — they were taped to cardboard tubes so we wouldn’t poke anyone’s eye out. That’s how hardcore we were. 2. Meet Officer Robocop Brain-Optional and His Magic Baton Okay, I’m going to make fun now. Forgive me, but some of it you earn. Every deployment has a Robocop Brain-Optional. You know him. Visor down even though it’s 34 degrees. Chest out. Baton twirling like he’s in a Michael Bay film. He didn’t join to protect. He joined because he liked the uniform in the mirror and because his cousin said you get respect without having to earn it. Field guide to Brain-Optional (subspecies: Escudus erectus ): Identified by shouting “MOVE BACK!” at people who are sitting. Believes a grandma with a Tupperware is a logistical threat. Thinks cameras are weapons. Thinks thinking is disobedience. His baton is magic: one tap turns a nurse into a “rioter,” a student into a “threat,” and his own paycheck into a lawsuit the city will pay, not him. That Tuesday, Brain-Optional found his nemesis: Dona Lurdes. She offered him a cookie. I saw it. “Son, you look hot, eat.” He shouted “DO NOT APPROACH!” She’s 68, 1.58m, approach speed: glacier. He pushed her sign. The sign said “COOKIES FOR FAIR WAGES.” Extremely subversive pastry. Here’s the provocative part, and I mean it: if your threat assessment flags cookies, you are not in security. You are in comedy. And it’s expensive comedy. One shove, one old lady on the ground, ten phones filming, and boom — you just turned 300 peaceful nobodies into 30,000 angry somebodies by tomorrow. Congratulations, genius. You created the danger you were sent to prevent. I’m not saying all cops are like this. I’m saying the ones who are, are loud, hit first, and hide behind the good ones when the video goes viral. And commanders love them until the lawsuit, then they’ve “never seen this officer before in their lives.” 3. Anatomy of Stupidity: Why Beating Peaceful People Is Tactically Idiotic Let me put my teacher hat on, because this story has to teach something useful or it’s just bar talk. Beating a peaceful manifestation is stupid on five levels. Write them down: 1. It doesn’t work. You don’t disperse ideas with bruises. You water them. Every textbook on crowd psychology — and every grandma — knows this. Hit a sitting kid and his entire school shows up next day. Gas a square and you get three squares. 2. It’s expensive. Overtime, medical bills, broken shields, lawsuits, burnt vans next week when people actually get mad. The city pays. That means you pay, even if you cheered for the beating on TV. The baton always bills the taxpayer. 3. It blinds you. Once you start hitting, you can’t tell who is actually dangerous. The one guy who did bring a Molotov hides behind the chaos you created. Good policing is like good surgery: don’t cut everything because one tooth is rotten. 4. It corrupts rookies. The 22-year-old who joined to help finds himself ordered to shove a teacher. He either obeys and hates himself, or disobeys and gets punished. You just taught him law is about obedience, not justice. Ten years later he’s Brain-Optional 2.0. 5. It’s cowardly math. 20 armored cops vs. one kid with a drum is not bravery. Real bravery is standing between traffic and marchers so nobody gets run over. Real bravery is telling your lieutenant “sir, these people are sitting, there’s no lawful reason to charge.” Kid with drum to cop line: “Why are you in armor? We’re not even in tune.” Cop (honest one, whispering): “Tell me about it. I told them we needed water, not shields.” Peaceful crowds are not dangerous. They are inconvenient. They block traffic. They chant off-key. They make politicians uncomfortable. Inconvenience is not danger. If your training confuses the two, your training is the danger. 4. Meet Dona Lurdes, 68, Terrorist Threat Level: Cookies Dona Lurdes is real. I changed her name a little because she’d kill me if I put her address, but everything else is true. Retired cook, widow, knees bad, voice loud. She brings cookies to every march because “people with low sugar make bad decisions — including police.” When Brain-Optional pushed her, she did not throw a brick. She sat down harder. Gravity as resistance. Then she said the most dangerous sentence of the day: “Son, I pay your salary, and I’m disappointed.” Ten phones caught it. That line did more damage to violent policing than any barricade. Humor is a weapon here, and I mean it as tactic: peaceful ridicule exposes stupidity without giving excuse for beating. When cops in armor face grandmas with cookies, who looks strong? Not the armor. My advice to every march: bring grandmas to the front. Not as shields — as mirrors. No officer wants to explain to his own mother why he pepper-sprayed someone’s mother over cardboard. Dona Lurdes later filed a complaint. With receipt for cookies. “Item: 40 cookies, wasted due to shove.” The clerk laughed, then stamped it. Paper is slow, but paper remembers when bruises fade. Keep receipts. Literally. 5. The Other Cop: Mario, Who Reads Orders Twice Now the other side, because I promised, and because it’s true. Mario is 41, two kids, belly from station coffee, 17 years on the force. He was in that line too. Helmet under arm because “if I can’t see faces, I can’t do my job.” When lieutenant shouted “Push them back to the avenue,” Mario did something revolutionary: he looked. He saw kids sitting. Signs. Cookies on pavement. No bricks, no bottles, no knives. He leaned to the rookie next to him: “What exactly are we pushing? Air?” Then he did the four-word magic: walked to lieutenant and said, “Is that lawful, sir?” I didn’t hear it — a journalist friend told me later, and Mario confirmed over beer (he paid, good man). The lieutenant blinked. “It’s an order.” Mario: “Orders need legal basis, sir. What’s the infraction? Assembly is constitutional. No violence, no blockade of emergency route — we can reroute traffic in ten minutes. If we charge, we create the crime.” That pause saved the day from becoming a hospital night. The lieutenant, to his credit, hesitated. Hesitation is underrated. He radioed: “Hold line. No advance unless attacked.” Brain-Optional sulked. Mario handed Dona Lurdes back her Tupperware. Listen: police are useful — essential, even — but only when they question orders. A cop who obeys blindly is just a baton with legs. A cop who thinks is a citizen with authority. The first serves whoever shouts loudest. The second serves law. Lesson from Mario for every cop reading this (and I know some are): Your oath is to the constitution, not to the lieutenant’s mood. “I was following orders” stopped working as an excuse in 1945. If an order tells you to beat peaceful people, that order is unlawful. Refusing it is not disobedience — it’s obedience to higher law. And yes, it takes guts. So does getting hit with a brick, and you signed up for guts. 6. Useful Police 101: What Cops Are Actually For (Hint: Not Piñata Duty) Let’s be provocative but fair: we need police. I need them. You need them. The street vendor needs them when someone actually robs him. The march needs them when a drunk driver tries to plow through. My daughter needs them when she walks home at night. But useful police at a peaceful manifestation do four boring, beautiful things: 1. Protect the march from traffic and from provocateurs. Stand on the edges, backs to protesters, eyes outward. The best cop at a demo is the one you barely notice because he’s stopping cars, not swinging. 2. Talk. “Hey, organizers, where are you heading? Let’s keep one lane open for ambulances, deal?” Ten minutes of talk saves ten hours of ER. Mario does this. Brain-Optional thinks talking is weakness. Talking is tactics. 3. Target only real violence, precisely. If one idiot throws a bottle, you pull that idiot — with minimum force, on camera — not gas the 299 others. Collective punishment is for bad parents, not professionals. 4. Document for truth. Bodycams on. Not off when it gets interesting. A good cop wants footage because footage proves he was good. I once saw Mario carry that kid-with-drum’s drum over a puddle so it wouldn’t get wet. The crowd laughed, clapped. Next chant was “MARIO! MARIO!” He blushed under his cap. That’s authority. Not fear — trust. Fear needs armor. Trust just needs consistency. So yeah, mock the stupid, but recruit the useful. When you chant “cops are...” — finish it with “welcome if they protect.” It confuses Brain-Optional and delights Mario. Provocation with precision. 7. The Order: “Disperse Them” — And The Four Words That Save Lives Every abuse starts with vague words on a radio. “Disperse.” “Clear.” “Restore order.” Order of what? There was order — sitting order, singing order. Here’s what I teach in workshops now (yes, I do them in community halls with bad coffee, come): For cops: the 30-second legality check. 1. What law is being broken, specifically? (Noise after 10pm is not “riot.” Sitting is not “attack.”) 2. Is my action proportionate and necessary? (Baton vs. cardboard = no. Shield wall vs. sitting = no.) 3. Did I warn clearly, give time and exit path? (“Disperse in 2 minutes via north street, water station there” — not a scream while charging.) 4. Would I do this if my mother and my chief were both filming? (They are. Phones everywhere.) If any answer is no — hold, ask, document refusal of unlawful order. Write it. Paper protects thinkers. Mario told me his trick: he repeats the order back loudly. “Sir, confirm: you want us to use force against seated, non-violent people with no emergency blockade?” Nine times out of ten, the commander rephrases to something lawful, because now it’s on record. Bureaucracy, used for good. Beautiful. And commanders: if you give an order you wouldn’t sign with your name in the newspaper tomorrow, don’t give it. “Just clear them, I don’t care how” means “I want violence without responsibility.” Courts translate that now. So do mothers. 8. What Protesters Can Do So Even Dumb Policing Fails Story time again, because preaching bores even me. After the cookie incident, we got smart. Not paranoid — organized. Old Man Joaquim, ex-army, became our “Mario on our side.” He taught: Know the line. March permit? Route? Time? Print it. Give copy to police liaison. When you’re clearly legal, unlawful orders stand out like a baton in a bakery. De-escalation team with vests. Our team wore yellow vests: “PEACE TEAM.” Their job: hug the hotheads (metaphorically), talk down the drunk guy, pull back the kid who wants to throw. They also filmed everything — two phones per team, power banks, livestream. Brain-Optional hates livestream the way vampires hate garlic. Grandmas front, sound truck middle, medics back. Front line sitting if charged. Hands up, palms open. Chant: “We are peaceful — film this.” It’s hard to beat people chanting they’re peaceful while sitting. It looks exactly like what it is. No masks for throwing, no sticks, no bottles. We banned them ourselves. Anyone masked and throwing was isolated — our peace team pointed: “That guy is not with us.” That denies police the excuse of “mixed violent crowd.” It also protects us from infiltrators who love a good smash. Talk to Mario before march. We started meeting the station a day before. “We’ll be 500, route X, end 8pm, our liaison is Ana with red cap, yours?” Most cops relaxed visibly. Only Brain-Optional was disappointed — no war, no story for the bar. Ana (red cap) to line: “Officers, we’ll keep right lane free, kids in middle, we end at 8, okay?” Mario: “Deal. I’ll put two guys at the intersection so buses pass.” Brain-Optional: “...” (kicking pebble, dreaming of riot) Useful lesson: discipline is our shield. Humor is our sword. Cameras are our witnesses. Paper is our revenge. 9. What Commanders Fear More Than Bricks: Cameras, Grandmas, and Paperwork Let me be blunt, human to human: commanders don’t fear your chant. They fear your folder. After Dona Lurdes fell, Ana did three things that night that scared the station more than any brick: uploaded video with time-stamp, took Lurdes to clinic for a report (bruise, shock), and filed a complaint with number, names, badge numbers she’d memorized by flirting with Mario (“for the report, handsome, your badge?” — he laughed and gave it, because good cops aren’t afraid of names). That folder grew: 12 videos, 3 medical reports, 1 cookie receipt, 40 witness contacts. It went to the ombudsman, the press, the councilwoman. The lieutenant who ordered “push” got called to explain. Brain-Optional got “reassigned to traffic” — which is where he now tickets pigeons, allegedly. Provocative truth: one grandma with a folder beats ten kids with stones. Stones give excuse. Folders give consequences. Be the folder. And cops, listen: the folder protects you too. Mario’s bodycam and written “Is that lawful, sir?” saved him when the inquiry came. The inquiry saw who held line and who pushed. Paper distinguishes Mario from Brain-Optional when headlines blur. If you’re good, you want more paper, not less. 10. The Night Nobody Got Hit — A Manual in Story Form Three months later, same square, 2000 people now — because stupidity recruits. Big march. Everyone expected war. Vans again. Same lieutenant, wiser. Same Mario, calmer. Same Brain-Optional, traffic cone in hand. What happened? Boring. Gloriously boring. 5pm: Ana meets lieutenant, hands route, liaison numbers. Lieutenant: “North street must stay open for hospital.” Ana: “Done, our yellow vests will keep it.” Mario nods. 6pm: March starts. Peace team in yellow. Grandmas front with cookies (extra for cops — diplomacy via sugar). Medics back with red crosses. Livestreamers on ladders. 6:40pm: One masked kid throws a bottle. Misses. Our peace team surrounds him, takes bottle, points to police: “Him, not us. We’ll testify.” Mario’s squad pulls him precisely, no gas, no charge. Crowd claps. Yes, claps for an arrest — because it was fair. 7:30pm: Provocateur shouts “Pigs!” in Mario’s face, spitting. Mario: “Sir, step back, you’re free to shout from there.” No baton. Spit wiped. Dignity kept. The crowd chants “MA-RI-O!” The provocateur looks stupid, leaves. 8pm: Ends on time. Trash picked up by us (revolutionary hygiene). Lieutenant on radio: “Crowd dispersing voluntarily. No force used.” He sounds almost disappointed and relieved at once. No one hit. No one gassed. Traffic resumed. Cookies shared. Pigeons fed. Manual hidden in story: Liaison + legal route + internal discipline + precise policing + cameras + humor = boring night. Boring is victory. If you want exciting protests, let Brain-Optional command. If you want change, be boring and relentless. Power hates boring persistence more than exciting riots — riots end, persistence votes, sues, elects. I cried a little that night, not ashamed to say. Not from gas. From relief. My neighbor’s kid on shoulders again, waving at Mario. Mario waving back. That’s the country I want. 11. Law Without Latin: Your Rights, Their Limits, and The Paper That Bites Back I’m not a lawyer — I’m a guy who got tired of being shoved and read stuff at 2am. So plain words, check your local law because I’m not your lawyer: Peaceful assembly is a right, not a favor. Constitutions and human rights treaties protect it. Police need a real, specific, lawful reason to limit it — imminent violence, blocking ER access with no alternative — not “inconvenience” or “we don’t like chant.” Force must be legal, necessary, proportionate, warned. Baton against sitting = disproportionate. Gas without exit = trap. Shooting rubber at faces = crime. Orders to do those = unlawful — must be questioned, refused, reported. Film. In public you can generally film police doing duty. Keep distance, don’t interfere, state “I’m filming, not interfering.” Livestream so deletion fails. Badge numbers, times, streets — narrate them aloud on video. Complain fast, complain precise. Date, hour, place, badge, what happened, witnesses, medical report within 24h, keep clothes, keep cookie receipts. Ombudsman, prosecutor, press, council — same folder to all. Polite, stubborn, boring. Bureaucracy fears persistence. For cops: document your refusal of unlawful order in writing, same day, copy to union/lawyer. “At 18:12 ordered to charge seated crowd, no legal basis observed, requested clarification, held position per constitution Art. X.” That sentence is armor better than shield. Whistleblower protections exist — use them, find Mario-like seniors, journalists, inspectors before you’re ordered to be Brain-Optional. Law is slow. I know. Dona Lurdes waited 8 months for apology and compensation for cookies and bruise. But apology came, with stamp. And Brain-Optional’s record now has a line. Lines accumulate. Third line, he’s out. Paper bites, slowly, but it doesn’t let go. 12. Epilogue: A Pact Between The Square and The Shield Last month I had coffee with Mario. Real coffee, not station mud. He said: “You make us look dumb in your stories.” I said: “Only the dumb ones. You look good.” He laughed: “My kids read it. My son wants to be peace-team when he grows up. My daughter wants to be lawyer for grandmas.” Dona Lurdes still marches. Knees worse, cookies better. Brain-Optional still directs traffic. Last week he helped her cross the street. She offered cookie. He refused, then accepted. Progress. So here’s the pact I propose, human to human, no AI-speak, no podium: The Square–Shield Pact (copy, sign, stick on fridge, station wall): We, protesters, promise peaceful, organized, disciplined marches — no bricks, no masks for violence, liaison, lanes for ambulances, cameras on, humor sharp, folders ready. We, police, promise protection, not provocation — backs to marchers, eyes outward, talk first, minimum precise force only against real violence, cams on, orders questioned when unlawful, names visible. povertyAndFaith: Home Monkey Blog · Data Dossier · Dossier de Dados English Português Politics, Law & Justice · Data Dossier The Poor and the Faithful A serious answer to a question many people carry silently: is it my impression, or is poverty in Muslim countries less harsh and less radical than in Christian countries? The honest answer needs numbers, real examples on both sides, and one distinction that almost every argument about this skips. Poverty Religion & data Welfare Muslim-majority countries Christian-majority countries Bilingual 1. The claim, stated properly The question, as it is usually asked in Portuguese, runs like this: «Será impressão minha ou nos países muçulmanos a pobreza não chega a ser tão dura e tão radical, quanto aos países cristãos?» — is it my impression, or in Muslim countries does poverty not become as hard and as radical as in Christian countries? It deserves a straight answer, because the question underneath it is legitimate even when its framing is not: people notice that the poorest places they hear about in the news are often Christian-majority (Haiti, the favelas of Brazil, the street homeless of Los Angeles) and that the Muslim-majority countries they see in images look organised, hospitable and often rich (Doha, Dubai, Istanbul). Both observations are real. Neither one is evidence. Three clarifications before the data, because they decide everything that follows. An impression measures visibility, not poverty. What you can see is filtered by press freedom, by whether begging is tolerated in public, by where tourists are taken, and by which disasters get cameras. Extreme rural poverty in the Sahel, in Afghanistan or in Bangladesh is far less photogenic than a tent on a Los Angeles pavement. "Muslim countries" and "Christian countries" are not comparable units. There are around fifty Muslim-majority states, several of them among the richest on earth per person and several among the poorest. Christianity is the majority religion in roughly half the planet's countries — Norway, Haiti, the Philippines, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United States are all in the same group. Any average across such a group hides more than it shows. Poverty is not a religion and religion is not an income. The measurable drivers of destitution are the ones the World Bank, the UN and national statistical offices keep testing: state capacity, conflict, growth, the distribution of land and oil rents, education, health systems, jobs and social transfers. Religion can shape some of those — through charity institutions, family norms, law — but it is not the variable that does most of the work, and no dataset has ever shown that it is. So this dossier does three things: it gives the numbers for both groups, it takes the part of the question that is defensible and shows exactly what produces it, and it names the part that is not defensible. It is not an attack on the question. It is an attempt to answer it better than it was asked. 2. How poverty is measured, and why that decides the answer Almost every dispute about "which poverty is worse" is really a dispute about the instrument. There are four instruments in common use, and each one is honest about something different. The international poverty line. The World Bank anchors it to the national poverty lines of the poorest countries. In June 2025 it was updated to $3.00 per person per day (2021 prices), replacing the old $2.15 line. It measures whether a household can buy a survival basket of food and essentials. It says nothing about dignity, debt, housing quality or safety. The multidimensional poverty index (MPI). Built by UNDP and OPHI, it counts deprivations in health, education and living standards — nutrition, child mortality, years of schooling, school attendance, cooking fuel, sanitation, water, electricity, housing, assets. It catches the poverty that a market basket misses, and it is the measure in which "poverty is harsh" is most visible. National poverty lines. Each country's own threshold. Useful for trend, useless for comparison: the Philippines' 15.5 per cent in 2023 and Yemen's 74 per cent in 2022 are not measuring the same basket of goods. Relative poverty , used by the OECD (below half the median income of the country). This is the measure that shows poverty in rich countries — the reason Israel can record 21 per cent poor in 2024 and the United States 10.6 per cent in 2024 while Yemen records 74 per cent. The consequence is blunt: a Christian-majority country with a weak welfare state and high inequality will look poor on the relative measure and fine on the absolute one; a Muslim-majority rentier state with oil money and a tiny citizen population will look rich on both while holding hundreds of thousands of migrant workers outside its social contract entirely. If the question uses "poor" to mean "living on very little money" the answer comes from the first two instruments. If it uses "poor" to mean "falling behind the neighbours you can see", it comes from the fourth, and then the comparison is between welfare states. The same two countries can swap places depending on which line you draw. That is not a scandal about the data; it is the reason any honest answer has to name its measure out loud. 3. The numbers, side by side Three global facts frame everything below. In 2026, about 811 million people — one in ten — live on less than $3.00 a day , a rate essentially unchanged since 2019; more than half of the world's extreme poor live in just nine economies ; and by 2030 about 87 per cent are projected to live in Sub-Saharan Africa or in fragile and conflict-affected states. On the multidimensional measure, 1.2 billion people out of 6.3 billion (18.9 per cent) in 108 countries are in acute multidimensional poverty — the first rise since the index began in 2010 — with 616 million of them in Sub-Saharan Africa (51.4 per cent of its population); more than half of all the multidimensionally poor are children, and eight in ten live in rural areas. The table is a selection of real, documented cases, not a ranking. The filter below the caption switches between the groups. In the first four rows a Muslim-majority country shows some of the harshest poverty recorded anywhere on earth: three quarters of Yemen and of Afghanistan, and the entire population of Gaza. In the next rows another Muslim-majority country shows the opposite extreme, and a fifth — Indonesia — has built a health insurer covering 98 per cent of its population. On the Christian side the same spread appears: the Democratic Republic of the Congo at 69 per cent and Ethiopia at 43 per cent against the United States at 10.6 per cent, with Haiti at the bottom of its hemisphere. And the single largest poverty reduction in the table, India's, happened in a Hindu-majority country. 4. The finding: the difference inside each group is bigger than the difference between them Take the two groups as people usually mean them. Inside the Muslim-majority group, income per person runs from roughly a few hundred dollars a year in Afghanistan to above thirty thousand in Saudi Arabia and above eighty thousand in Qatar: a factor of two hundred between two states that share the same majority religion and, in some cases, the same legal tradition. Inside the Christian-majority group the same spread appears: Norway, Denmark and Switzerland at the top of every human-development table, the Democratic Republic of the Congo at 69 per cent below the national poverty line and Haiti the poorest country in its hemisphere. That spread is the whole answer to the original question, and it is not a rhetorical trick. It is what the World Bank's own data show when you stop averaging: poverty is not distributed by creed, it is distributed by geography, conflict and rent. In 2026 more than half of the world's extremely poor live in nine economies — a set that includes Muslim-majority, Hindu-majority and mixed states — and by 2030 about 87 per cent of them are projected to be in Sub-Saharan Africa or in fragile and conflict-affected situations. On the multidimensional measure, the deepest concentration on earth is Sub-Saharan Africa, with 616 million people (51.4 per cent) — a region that is roughly half Muslim and half Christian. Africa does not sort by religion. It sorts by war, by colonial borders, by commodity prices and by the capacity of a state to collect taxes and deliver services. Three consequences follow, and they are worth saying plainly. One Muslim-majority country cannot be compared with one Christian-majority country, and neither can the averages. With roughly fifty Muslim-majority states and about half the world's countries being Christian-majority, the groups contain both the richest societies ever measured and some of the poorest. The comparison people actually make is between subsets. In practice the eye compares the Gulf with Haiti, or Istanbul with a favela in Rio. Those are real photographs, but they are comparing the wealthiest corner of one group with the poorest corner of the other. The strongest correlates of destitution are known and boring: war, state capacity, dependence on a single commodity, tropical disease burden, isolation from markets, education, and whether women are permitted or able to work. The World Bank's 2026 assessment put a number on the last one: raising employment in poor households, including by closing the gender gap, would cut global extreme poverty by roughly a fifth. If the same religion produces both the richest and the poorest states in the file, then religion is not the variable doing the work. Something else is, and that something else is what this dossier is searching for. 5. Where the impression is half right — three real mechanisms There is a defensible version of the question, and it deserves real examples rather than a shrug. Three mechanisms genuinely soften the edge of poverty in specific Muslim-majority countries. None of them is the religion itself, and all three have Christian-majority equivalents or failures. A. Rent shared with citizens The Gulf states built their welfare on hydrocarbons: free or cheap energy and water, subsidised food, guaranteed public-sector jobs, no income tax, generous family allowances, and — after the price reforms — explicit cash compensation. Saudi Arabia's Citizen's Account , introduced with the 2018 round of energy reforms, was designed precisely to keep low- and middle-income households whole after the price rises; Iran did the same thing on a bigger scale in 2010, when it raised energy prices to market levels and paid a monthly transfer to almost every citizen (445,000 rials per person per month at the time), which economists still study as the largest such swap ever attempted. The result is real: some of the least visible poverty on earth, among citizens. The mechanism is the rent, not the faith. The proof is the rest of the class: Nigeria, Iraq, Angola, Libya and Algeria are oil states with mass poverty; Venezuela and Equatorial Guinea are oil states in other religious categories with the same result. Oil money makes a state generous to its own population when the population is small, and it does nothing of the kind when it is large or when the money is captured. B. Obligatory almsgiving and endowed charity as institutions Zakat is the most interesting of the three, because it has no exact Christian equivalent: it is a compulsory levy , commonly 2.5 per cent of qualifying wealth, and in several countries the state collects it. In Pakistan it is deducted at source from bank accounts; in Saudi Arabia, Malaysia and Sudan it is collected by official bodies; Indonesia has a national agency (BAZNAS) that reported around Rp 32.3 trillion collected in 2023 against an estimated national potential several times larger. Global estimates of annual zakat flows range from $200 billion to $1 trillion (a UNDP estimate quoted in the Islamic Development Bank's own materials) to $550–600 billion (a UN-ESCWA compilation). Even the lowest figure dwarfs global humanitarian aid. Historically the same logic ran through the waqf , the charitable endowment: hospitals, schools, fountains, soup kitchens and caravanserais financed by assets locked out of inheritance. Compare the instruments honestly: Christian charity has the tithe, the parish, the religious order and the relief agency — Caritas, the Salvation Army, the food banks — and these are voluntary or congregational, not a levy with state collection. That difference is real. What it produces, however, is not a gentler poverty but a different plumbing of relief. Egypt's Takaful and Karama transfers went from about 1 million households in 2018 to 4.5 million in 2025 ; Pakistan's BISP reaches many millions of households and is the country's largest social assistance programme; Indonesia's JKN health scheme covers 280 million people, about 98 per cent of the population . Those are state programmes funded by taxation and transfers as much as by alms, and they exist alongside zakat rather than instead of it. C. Family absorption, remittances and the taboo on visible begging The third mechanism is the household. In many Muslim-majority societies the informal obligation to feed a cousin, to host a relative, to send money home from the Gulf, is strong and enforceable through honour. Egypt, Pakistan and Bangladesh are among the world's largest recipients of worker remittances; a house in Kerala or a shop in Sylhet may be financed entirely by a brother abroad. Together with the norm that begging is shameful and should be handled privately or through the mosque, this produces something measurable and something optical at the same time. The measurable part is real relief to millions of people. The optical part is the point of this whole dossier: the same mechanism that genuinely softens some poverty also hides it. Poverty absorbed inside a family, a village or a mosque network does not appear on the pavement, so a foreign visitor does not see it. That is what produces the impression in the question, and it is also why the multidimensional index — which counts sanitation, schooling, fuel, nutrition, child mortality — repeatedly finds severe deprivation in countries whose streets look calm. One more equality, to keep the ledger straight: the world's most effective anti-poverty programmes of the last thirty years came mostly out of two traditions — the Nordic welfare state and the Latin American conditional cash transfer. Bolsa Família in Brazil, a Christian-majority country, kept 8.6 million people out of poverty between 2023 and 2024; without the social programmes, Brazil's extreme poverty rate would have been 10.0 per cent instead of 3.5 per cent. Mexico's Progresa-Oportunidades exported the model to dozens of countries. Bangladesh's BRAC exported its own: the Graduation approach, which lifts ultra-poor households out of destitution with assets, training and a stipend, and now runs in dozens of countries of every religion. 6. Where the impression breaks — the same countries, worst cases Now the other half of the same group. If the question were true as stated, the following situations should not exist. They do. Yemen. A Muslim-majority country in which 74 per cent of the population was below the national poverty line in 2022 (World Bank) and 82.7 per cent were multidimensionally poor in 2024 (UNDP). It is hard to find a harsher, more radical poverty on the planet, at any latitude. Afghanistan. Three out of four people unable to meet their basic needs in 2025, according to UNDP's own socioeconomic review — a figure that would have been called unthinkable in 2001. Gaza. UNCTAD's assessment in November 2025 found the economy collapsed by 83 per cent in 2024 and the entire population — 2.3 million people — below the poverty line. A UN report in July 2025 put poverty in Gaza near 100 per cent, up from 64 per cent before the war. The Sahel and the Horn. Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso, Chad and Somalia are Muslim-majority and among the poorest states in the world; the Sahel concentrates jihadist war, drought, displaced populations and state collapse. Somalia is routinely listed by World Bank-based compilations among the ten poorest countries on earth. South Asia. Bangladesh's programmes exist precisely because ultra-poverty there was extreme — people living on less than the cost of a minimum food basket, sleeping hungry, without assets. Pakistan's rural poverty and northern Nigeria's deprivation are of the same severity. The Gulf's own excluded class. This is the sharpest counterexample of all. In 2019 the ILO counted 24.1 million migrant workers in the Arab States , most of them in the Gulf, most of them from Muslim-majority countries themselves — Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, Indonesia, Egypt, Ethiopia. They build the cities, clean the houses and dig the foundations, they are usually excluded from the welfare, the subsidies, the citizenship and often the labour law, and their status can depend on a single employer under the sponsorship system. A poverty that is real, but kept off the census and off the pavement. The pattern in that list is not religion. It is war and state failure (Yemen, Afghanistan, Gaza, Somalia, Mali), plus the exclusion of non-citizens from a welfare state whose benefits were never designed for them. Both of those mechanisms exist in Christian-majority countries too — in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in Haiti, in Guatemala, among migrant workers in the United States and in the Gulf of the Christian Atlantic. 7. The Christian-majority side of the same pattern To answer the question fairly, the comparison has to be run in both directions, with the same instruments. The least poverty ever measured is Christian-majority — and it is not charity Norway, Denmark, Finland and Iceland are Lutheran-majority societies with the lowest poverty rates in the historical record, and the mechanism is not religious: it is state capacity. They tax around half of national income, deliver universal services, insure wages, and let the state, not the family or the parish, absorb shocks. Across the OECD, public social spending averaged about 21 per cent of GDP in 2024 , with Austria, Finland and France above 30 per cent. That is the strongest single finding in the whole comparison — and it is a finding about institutions, not about the Gospel. Foi, ao longo de toda a história recente, a presença policial nas grandes cidades — sobretudo Lisboa e Porto — ao contrário da GNR, que cobria o interior, as estradas e o litoral. Essa distinção não é apenas geográfica: é uma distinção de ritmo, de perfil e de pressão. Uma polícia de cidade vive o chão de rua, freguesia a freguesia, o trânsito, o mercado, a proximidade e o barulho de quem está sempre à porta. Durante o Estado Novo, a PSP, como todas as forças de segurança, funcionou dentro de uma ordem política autoritária. É uma parte da história que não se pode apagar nem glorificar demais: a instituição serviu o regime da mesma maneira que serviria a República depois, porque é uma instituição estrutural, não uma ideologia. Distinguir isso não é pedantismo; é o primeiro exercício de leitura honesta de qualquer dossiê sobre polícia. O dragão da GNR escreveu sobre essa linha antes, com um tom que não esconde a tensão: GNR — O Dragão que Guarda a Lei . 1832 A Guarda Nacional surge Nasce com a necessidade de organizar a segurança nas cidades e nos espaços de conflito do século XIX. O nome e a estrutura vão mudando, mas a função urbana deixa marcas. 1900s–1930s A PSP consolida-se A polícia de Lisboa e Porto ganha maior capacidade de intervenção urbana, com unidades que antes eram mais dispersas a tornarem-se instituições de presença constante. 1933–1974 Estado Novo A PSP funciona no quadro de uma ditadura. Não é só "força de ordem" — é uma instituição envolvida na vida política, com o dever de obediência e a margem que toda a polícia tem. Um dossiê honesto não esconde essa linha; ela é o pano de fundo das perguntas sobre coragem e sobre obediência. 1974 em diante A democracia republicana Após o 25 de Abril, a PSP passa a fazer parte de uma ordem democrática com novas regras, novas expectativas e novas tensões entre obediência, lei e intervenção. Uma das perguntas que atravessa o dossiê não é apenas histórica. É ética. Se a polícia acata ordens, até quando acata? Se acata sempre, até que ponto foi "força pública" em vez de "braço do poder"? O blog já escreveu sobre essa questão com outra inclinação, num tom que mistura sistema, ética e ironia: Discurso do Eterno Macaco às Forças de Segurança do Mundo . A leitura completa ajuda a entender que a PSP nunca é só um braço; às vezes é o reflexo de um país inteiro. 02 · SÍMBOLOS O Tigre: três línguas, um animal O Tigre da PSP não é um acidente gráfico. É um animal que carrega coragem, força e presença; é também um símbolo que, em Portugal e na Ásia, fala línguas muito diferentes. Por isso é normal que o mesmo símbolo soe diferente dependendo de quem o olha e de onde o olha. Daqui nasce uma das lições centrais deste artigo: o símbolo não é uma tradução, é um convite para ler o contexto. Em Portugal, o tigre evoca a proeza, a vigília, a rapidez, a força necessária para a rua e para a crise. Isso não significa que seja "o animal do mal" ou "o animal da barbárie"; é um animal que, no imaginário público, tende a oscilar entre força necessária e força excessiva. Nesta página, trabalhamos essa dualidade de forma intencional: o tigre como coragem, não como crueldade, e reconhecendo que a crueldade existe e que a coragem, quando se desvia da sua função, pode tornar-se violência. Na Ásia, o tigre carrega um peso muito mais antigo e muito mais aberto. É um dos animais mais importantes da cultura chinesa, coreana, japonesa e vietnamita. Não é o dragão, que é celestial e raramente visto de perto. É o tigre: terrestre, audacioso, protetor em muitos contextos, símbolo de homens corajosos em outros, presença de bravura em gestos que exigem coragem e não apenas força. Quando se diz que o tigre é símbolo dos homens corajosos na Ásia, não é uma frase decorativa; é uma observação de que a coragem, na Ásia, está ligada ao animal que enfrenta, protege, avança e, em muitas lendas, não recua. 03 · ÁSIA Na Ásia, o tigre dos homens corajosos A afirmação de que "na Ásia também o Tigre é símbolo dos homens corajosos" é mais profunda do que parece. Na cartografia cultural asiática o tigre é, frequentemente, o animal que liga o homem à sua coragem de forma mais direta do que o dragão. O dragão é, em grande parte da Ásia, o poder celestial, a sabedoria, a água e a chuva, o que unifica e o que governa. O tigre é o corpo que age. É o animal que corre, que protege o território, que enfrenta o perigo, que não representa apenas o poder do céu, mas a coragem de quem está em terra firme. Na China, o tigre é um dos quatro animais sagrados, ao lado do dragão azul, da ave vermelha (fénix) e da tartaruga negra. O tigre azul (青虎) pode aparecer em muitas variantes; em algumas tradições é protetor, noutras é o animal que combate a energia negativa. Há um detalhe surpreendente na leitura ocidental comum: o tigre asiático não é apenas "o animal feroz". É a força que o homem cultiva para estar à frente do perigo sem se deixar levar por ele. Essa é a coragem que interessa a este artigo: não a força que ataca, mas a coragem que enfrenta com responsabilidade. No Japão, o tigre aparece em mitologia, em trajes de teatro e em armaduras, como símbolo de proteção e bravura. Na Coreia, o tigre é, junto com o dragão, um dos dois animais que aparecem tanto na imagética protetora como na lenda. No Vietname, o tigre é fortemente associado à resistência e à coragem nacional. Em todas essas culturas, há uma linha comum: o tigre é usado para falar de homens que a exercem, não apenas de animais que fazem medo. Não é estranho, portanto, que uma polícia portuguesa use um tigre no seu emblema. O que é estranho — ou pelo menos controverso — é usar um símbolo associado à coragem e depois esquecer que a coragem exige limites. A diferença entre coragem e brutalidade é de intenção, de proporcionalidade, de cuidado com o inocente. Essa distinção é o trabalho central não só de um dossiê, mas de uma democracia que quer olhar para a sua polícia sem desviar os olhos nem usar a retórica para fechar os olhos. Comentário pedagógico — o símbolo como convite à introspecção O tigre da PSP não deve ser apenas uma imagem de força. Deve ser um lembrete de que a coragem de um homem está envolvida na coragem de um animal — a de avançar quando é necessário, a de recuar quando a lei e a dignidade exigem. Quando um símbolo de coragem é usado sem reflexão, corre-se o risco de transformar coragem em licença para hiper-reacção. Por isso, ler símbolos de força pública exige mais que admiração: exige a pergunta sobre os limites. python-cli: Monkey Blog · The Shell, Extended Home EN PT Terminal tools · a manual in nineteen parts The Shell, Extended Python's best software does not live in an app store. It lives in a terminal, in a repository with a README, behind one command that installs it. This manual is about that command: how to build a virtual environment, how to keep it out of the system, and thirty real GitHub projects worth the trouble — from posting to Mastodon to OCR on a scanned contract. Nineteen parts Thirty apps venv · pipx · uv Install builder Ten errors, solved Every repo linked I have never made a venv Part 02: seven commands, one afternoon, and nothing else on your machine changes. Show me the tools first Part 06: every tool with its package, version, home page and one-line purpose, plus the command for your machine. Just give me the command Part 03: one isolated environment per app, and no dependency conflicts. An install just failed Part 16: the ten messages that stop people, and the fix for each one. 01 Never install into the system Python Almost every broken Python install starts with one of two sentences: "it worked on my machine" and "I ran it with sudo". Both are the same mistake — installing a project's dependencies into the one interpreter your operating system uses to run itself. There is a rule that removes the whole class of problem, and it fits in three lines. One: the system Python belongs to the system Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, macOS and Arch all ship Python because parts of the operating system are written in it. Installing packages into it means two projects can demand two versions of the same library, and the loser is usually your desktop. Modern distributions now refuse: pip exits with error: externally-managed-environment , which is not a bug, it is a locked door with a reason. Two: a project gets a venv, an app gets pipx If you will import the thing from your own code, it belongs in a virtual environment inside the project folder. If you will only type its name at the prompt, it belongs in pipx (or uv), which gives the app its own private venv and puts a single launcher on your PATH. Nothing else on the machine sees it. Three: no sudo, ever, for pip The single exception is your distribution's package manager — apt install python3-venv , dnf install python3-pip — which installs the tooling, never a project's dependencies. If a README tells you to sudo pip install , the README is old; use the project's pyproject or the PyPI name with pipx. What that error actually says PEP 668 lets a distribution mark its interpreter as externally managed, with an EXTERNALLY-MANAGED marker file next to the standard library. pip reads it and stops. You can override it with --break-system-packages ; you should not, and no command in this manual needs it. The escape hatch is a venv, which is one command away. Three tools, three jobs Tool What it is for Use it when What it costs venv A folder with its own Python, its own pip and its own site-packages. Built into Python since 3.3. You are writing code that imports the library, or you need an exact pinned set of versions for one project. 20–200 MB per environment, and one activation command per terminal. pipx A manager of isolated environments, one per command-line app, with a launcher symlinked into ~/.local/bin . The package provides a command you run (yt-dlp, toot, csvkit) and you never import it. A few MB per app; the disk cost is the price of never having a dependency conflict again. uv A single fast binary that does venvs, pip installs, Python version downloads and tool installs — the same jobs, in seconds. You install tools often, or you are tired of waiting for a resolver. uvx also runs an app without installing it at all. One more binary to trust and to update; it is written in Rust, not Python. The whole idea, on one screen One environment per app, no activation needed, and the command is addressed by its full path. This is the pattern the rest of the manual refines; everything else is convenience built on top of it. python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/media ~/.venvs/media/bin/pip install --upgrade pip ~/.venvs/media/bin/pip install yt-dlp ~/.venvs/media/bin/yt-dlp --version Nothing was installed system-wide, nothing needs sudo, and deleting ~/.venvs/media removes every trace. The three drawbacks are that the path is long, that each app needs its own folder, and that you have to remember which folder holds what — which is exactly what pipx removes. 02 The virtual environment, from zero A venv is not a virtual machine and it is not magic: it is a directory containing a symlink to your Python, a copy of the launcher scripts, and a site-packages folder that pip writes into. Activating it changes one environment variable, PATH , so that python means this folder instead of the system one. That is the entire mechanism. Seven commands, in order Check what you have python3 --version should print 3.11 or newer for most of the apps in this manual (mitmproxy, for one, wants 3.12 — each project states its floor on PyPI). If the version is older than a project needs, install a newer interpreter next to the old one rather than replacing the system's. Install the venv module, if your distribution split it out Debian and Ubuntu ship Python without ensurepip , which makes python3 -m venv fail with "ensurepip is not available". One package fixes it permanently: sudo apt install python3-venv . Fedora and Arch already include it; macOS from python.org includes it; Homebrew's Python does too. Create it inside the project Name it .venv and put it in the project root — editors, linters and every tutorial already look there. The folder is disposable: no data lives in it, only symlinks and wheels. Activate it Activation is a convenience, not a requirement. It exists so that typing python and pip does the right thing; the environment works identically if you call .venv/bin/python directly, which is what cron jobs and scripts should do. Install with pip, then freeze Install what you need, confirm it imports, then write the exact versions to a file. pip freeze records everything including transitive dependencies; a hand-written requirements.txt records only your intent. For applications, freeze. For libraries, pin the direct dependencies and let the resolver work. Leave, and come back later deactivate restores the old PATH. Next session, activate again, or skip activation and use the full path. On a server, always skip it: a script that depends on an activated shell breaks the first time it runs from cron. Delete it when it rots When upgrades go wrong, the fastest fix is rm -rf .venv and create it again from requirements.txt . Ten seconds, no residue. This is the habit that makes the rest of this manual safe: environments are cheap, so never repair one for an hour. The same three commands on each system System Create Activate Leave Linux / macOS (bash, zsh) python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate deactivate fish python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate.fish deactivate Windows (PowerShell) py -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 deactivate Windows (cmd) py -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\activate.bat deactivate PowerShell blocks the activation script By default Windows refuses to run Activate.ps1 because it is an unsigned script. The fix is per-user, not per-machine: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned . If you would rather not touch policy at all, call .venv\Scripts\python.exe directly and never activate. A real session, with the output it should give cd ~/projects/scrape python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install --upgrade pip pip install requests beautifulsoup4 python -c "import requests, bs4; print(requests.__version__, bs4.__version__)" pip freeze > requirements.txt deactivate From another machine, or after deleting the folder: python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate && pip install -r requirements.txt . That one line is the entire portability story of a Python project, and it is why requirements.txt is committed while .venv is not. What goes into git Commit requirements.txt (or pyproject.toml with a lock file). Never commit .venv : it contains absolute paths, platform-specific binaries and tens of megabytes. One line in .gitignore — .venv/ — prevents a hundred confusing clones. The two flags that cause trouble --system-site-packages lets an environment see the system's packages, which quietly reintroduces the conflict you were escaping. --without-pip creates an environment with no installer; you then need python -m ensurepip . Neither is needed for anything in this manual. 03 pipx: one command per app, no conflicts pipx is the answer to a specific question: what if I want the command, not the library? It creates a private venv for each app under ~/.local/pipx/venvs , installs the package there with the right interpreter, and symlinks only the launcher into ~/.local/bin . Two apps can then depend on two incompatible versions of the same library and neither notices the other exists. Start here # Debian / Ubuntu sudo apt install pipx # Fedora sudo dnf install pipx # macOS (Homebrew) brew install pipx # or, with any Python already installed python3 -m pip install --user pipx pipx ensurepath # open a new terminal, then pipx install toot toot --help ensurepath writes the PATH line in your shell's startup file. If the next shell still says command not found , the file was the wrong one — see part 05 — or the shell cached its command list and needs hash -r . The eight pipx commands worth memorising Command What it does Why you would type it pipx install NAME Creates a venv and links the launcher. The normal case. Add extras in quotes: pipx install "qrcode[pil]" . pipx list Shows every app, its version and its command names. When you cannot remember whether you already installed something. pipx upgrade NAME Upgrades that app only, in its own venv. yt-dlp and gallery-dl need this often: sites change weekly. pipx upgrade-all Upgrades every app pipx manages. A monthly habit, not a daily one. pipx uninstall NAME Removes the venv and the launcher. A clean removal with no leftovers in site-packages. pipx inject NAME PKG Adds a library to that app's venv. For plugins and optional backends, without touching other apps. pipx run NAME Runs the app in a temporary venv that is thrown away. Trying something once without committing to it. pipx reinstall NAME --python 3.12 Rebuilds that app's venv with another interpreter. When an app needs a newer (or older) Python than the default. The plugin pattern A command with an ecosystem — beets, llm, mkdocs — usually wants a plugin. Install the app, then pipx inject beets beets-fetchart . The plugin lands in the same private venv, so it cannot break any other tool, and pipx upgrade beets leaves it alone. When an app must not move pipx has no lock file by design: it is for tools you want current. If a version must be frozen — a publishing pipeline, a scraper with brittle selectors — use a venv with a pinned requirements file, or uv tool install NAME==1.2.3 , and treat it as a project rather than a tool. 04 uv: the same jobs, in seconds uv is a single binary from Astral that replaces the slow parts of the Python toolchain: creating environments, resolving dependencies, downloading interpreters, installing command-line tools. It is not a Python package (there is a pip-installable wheel, but the supported install is the binary), and it is the one tool in this manual that is worth learning for its own sake. # install the binary (Linux / macOS) curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh # a tool, isolated, with its launcher on PATH uv tool install yt-dlp uv tool list uv tool upgrade --all uv tool uninstall yt-dlp # run something once, without installing it uvx csvlook data.csv # a project environment, pip-compatible uv venv .venv uv pip install -r requirements.txt uv python install 3.12 uvx is the feature that changes habits uvx NAME downloads the app into a cached environment, runs it with the arguments you gave, and leaves your PATH untouched. For a one-off conversion, a single csvsql query or a quick gallery-dl run, that is faster than deciding whether you want the tool permanently. The cache means the second run is instant. pipx or uv? Both produce the same result: an isolated environment and a launcher in ~/.local/bin . pipx is the conservative choice — it is packaged by every major distribution, its behaviour is stable, and it only manages tools. uv is faster and broader, and it will also manage your project environments and Python versions, which is either convenient or one dependency too many, depending on your taste. The manual uses pipx in its commands and notes the uv equivalent; nothing here needs both. Task pipx uv Install a tool pipx install X uv tool install X Run once pipx run X uvx X Upgrade everything pipx upgrade-all uv tool upgrade --all Choose the interpreter --python 3.12 --python 3.12 Add a plugin pipx inject X Y uv tool install X --with Y Project environment not its job uv venv , uv pip 05 PATH, and where things actually go The most common failure in this manual is not a broken package. It is a correct install whose command cannot be found, because the launcher was written to a directory your shell does not search. Knowing the four directories removes the mystery. Directory What lives there Should you touch it? ~/.local/bin Launchers from pipx and uv, plus any pip install --user script. No — but it must be on PATH. This is the directory ensurepath adds. ~/.local/pipx/venvs/<app> The private environment of each pipx app, with its dependencies. Never by hand. pipx owns it; edit through inject or reinstall. ~/.venvs Environments that belong to no project — a scratch toolbox of your own. Yes, freely. It is just folders you invented; delete them when bored. /usr/local/bin System-wide launchers, usually from your distribution or a make install. Only with sudo, and only for things the package manager did not provide. Adding it once, per shell # bash — ~/.bashrc zsh — ~/.zshrc export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" # fish fish_add_path ~/.local/bin # then, in the current shell source ~/.bashrc command -v toot On Windows the equivalent is setx PATH "%PATH%;%USERPROFILE%\AppData\Roaming\Python\Scripts" in a fresh cmd, and a restart of the terminal. If command -v prints nothing but the file exists, the shell is using a cached list: hash -r in bash, rehash in zsh, or simply open a new window. The check that settles it ls ~/.local/bin | head shows whether the launcher exists; echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n' | grep local shows whether the shell looks there. Those two commands answer "why is my command not found" in five seconds, and they are always the first thing to run before reading an error message twice. 06 Build the command for your machine Three choices — the app, the method, the operating system — and the block below is what you paste. Between them, publishing and testing an endpoint stop being a reason to open a window. toot — a Mastodon client in the terminal A Python CLI for Mastodon and compatible servers (Pleroma, GoToSocial, Akkoma). It authenticates with an app token stored in your config, so the password never appears in a command line. It posts, threads, uploads media, reads timelines and can run scheduled posts through cron. pipx install toot toot login # choose the instance, paste the code toot post "first post from the shell" toot post "a thread" --visibility unlisted toot tui # a full terminal interface toot timeline --local --num 20 toot upload photo.jpg --description "a caption for screen readers" The TUI is the part people miss: toot tui gives a keyboard-driven timeline with replies and boosts, useful on a server over SSH. For automation, toot post returns the new status URL, so a script can chain it. posting — an API client that lives in the terminal Postman, for people who live in a shell: requests stored as YAML files in a collection, environments with variables, syntax highlighting, and keyboard-only editing. The Python distribution on PyPI is what pipx installs; the project's README documents the newer standalone binary if you prefer that route. HTTPie — the readable curl curl is always there and always cryptic. HTTPie turns a request into something closer to a sentence: JSON is assumed, headers are coloured, and the response is formatted instead of concatenated. If you have already leaked one, revoke it — do not edit the history and hope. 08 Media: download, archive, convert The most-installed command-line Python apps in the world are media downloaders, and for good reason: they do one job better than any website, they are scriptable, and they keep working after the site changes. All four here want ffmpeg installed by the system, not by pip — that is the single most common reason a download "succeeds" and produces no file. # the system dependency all four share sudo apt install ffmpeg # Debian / Ubuntu sudo dnf install ffmpeg # Fedora (RPM Fusion) brew install ffmpeg # macOS yt-dlp — the reference implementation of "download that" A fork of youtube-dl that is updated weekly and supports well over a thousand sites. Keep the archive file with the media, not in /tmp . gallery-dl — image galleries, not videos The companion tool for the sites yt-dlp does not cover: image boards, artist pages, manga readers, photo feeds. It preserves the post metadata as JSON next to the files, which makes an archive searchable years later. pipx install gallery-dl gallery-dl "https://example.com/artist" gallery-dl --range 1-50 "https://example.com/gallery" gallery-dl -g URL # print the URLs instead of downloading gallery-dl --write-metadata URL # JSON

Fifteen gated levels. Every gate must be passed before the next one opens. Level 00 Orientation not started ~14 min What Python actually is (and what it is not) Most Python damage happens before the first line of code: wrong interpreter, wrong environment, wrong expectations. Before touching an installer, build the mental model. Python is a language specification plus a reference implementation. CPython — the one you get from python.org , your distro, or uv — compiles your source to bytecode and executes it on a virtual machine. That distinction explains almost every confusing error message you will meet. The five things that exist on disk When you install "Python", you are really installing a layout. Learn it once and environment bugs stop being mysterious. python -m sysconfig | head -40 prints the real paths for the interpreter you are running. Interpreter anatomy Thing Typical Linux path What it means python3 /usr/bin/python3 The executable (often a symlink). Its version can differ from every other Python on the box. stdlib /usr/lib/python3.13/ Batteries included: json , pathlib , ssl , sqlite3 . Owned by the OS or installer. site-packages …/site-packages/ Third-party packages. This is the directory virtual environments exist to isolate. scripts/bin ~/.local/bin , .venv/bin Console entry points ( pytest , ruff ). Must be on PATH to be callable by name. config ~/.config/pip/pip.conf Index URLs, caches, credentials. A wrong setting here breaks every install silently. Four layers, one process Python code lives in a stack of layers. Bugs that look like "Python is broken" are nearly always a mismatch between two adjacent layers. Language — syntax and semantics. Versioned by minor release (3.12, 3.13, 3.14, 3.15). New syntax can be unavailable on older interpreters, which is why requires-python exists. Standard library — ships with the interpreter, has the same version number, and is not installable via pip. Never pip install json ; that package name is a squatter. Third-party packages — installed into a site-packages directory, resolved by sys.path order. Your project — source code plus a declaration of which of the above it needs. bash · confirm what you are actually running copy python3 -VV # e.g. Python 3.13.7 (main, ...) [GCC 14.2.0] which -a python3 python # every Python on PATH, in resolution order python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable); print(sys.prefix); print(sys.path)' That last command is the single most useful diagnostic in Python. sys.executable tells you which binary runs; sys.prefix tells you which environment it belongs to; sys.path tells you where imports will look, first match wins. If a package "is installed but cannot be imported", these three lines answer the question in seconds. Bad decision #0 — "Python is installed, so I can pip install anything" There are usually three or more Pythons on a modern Linux machine: the OS one ( /usr/bin/python3 ), a Homebrew or pyenv one, and one inside each project. pip on your PATH may belong to none of the ones you run. This is the root cause of the classic "I installed requests but Python says ModuleNotFoundError" . The fix is not to reinstall — it is to stop calling bare pip . Use python -m pip , or better, activate the project environment first. Then pip cannot point at the wrong interpreter, because it is the interpreter. Level 01–03 (install, configure, environments) are the foundation: skipping them is why so many tutorials fail on a real machine. Levels 04–06 are the language and standard library. Levels 07–08 are where careers are made — security and testing. Levels 09–11 cover the ecosystem, packaging, and the anti-patterns gallery. There are five legitimate strategies with different blast radii. Choosing the wrong one is how people end up with a broken desktop and a stack of Stack Overflow tabs. First, a rule that will save you hours: never let a project depend on the operating system's Python . Your distro uses Python for system tooling — package managers, drivers, desktop utilities. Treat /usr/bin/python3 as read-only infrastructure and install your own interpreter for your own work. Choose your strategy Installation strategies compared Strategy Best for Cost / risk OS packages apt , dnf , pacman Running distro tooling; quickly getting a Python for small scripts; servers with a strict "no unmanaged software" policy. Older version, patched by the distro, externally managed (PEP 668). You cannot pip-install into it. pyenv Needing several CPython versions per user; reproducing an old project; testing against 3.11–3.15. Compiles from source: needs build deps and ~5–15 min per version. Shims can confuse editors. uv python install The modern default for developer machines and CI. Fast, per-user, no root, no compile step. One more tool to learn; standalone builds may lag a patch release by days. Official installer (.pkg / .exe) Windows and macOS desktops, especially beginners; no compiler toolchain available. Manual upgrades; on Windows the PATH checkbox and the Microsoft Store alias are a classic trap. Containers python:3.13-slim Anything deployed; reproducible CI; "works on my machine" elimination. Not for day-to-day editing unless you wire volumes; image size and base-image patching are your job. Why "just use the latest" is not the whole answer Python's annual release cadence (October) means a brand-new minor version is often not yet supported by every C-extension you depend on. For production, the pragmatic choice in late 2026 is the newest version that your dependency set publishes wheels for — usually 3.13 or 3.14, moving to 3.15 after a few months. For learning, use the latest stable. Check the support table before you commit: 3.10 went end-of-life on 2026-10-01 and no longer receives security fixes. Linux: the distro route Debian and Ubuntu ship a solid CPython but split it across packages. The interpreter alone cannot create virtual environments — you need the venv module package, and pip is often absent by design. bash · Debian 12/13, Ubuntu 24.04+ copy sudo apt update sudo apt install -y python3 python3-venv python3-pip python3-dev build-essential python3 -VV python3 -m venv --help >/dev/null && echo "venv OK" bash · Fedora / RHEL family copy sudo dnf install -y python3 python3-pip python3-devel gcc redhat-rpm-config # Versioned interpreters are separate packages, e.g.: sudo dnf install -y python3.13 python3.13-pip bash · Arch copy sudo pacman -S --needed python python-pip # Arch tracks the latest release; do not partial-upgrade around it. On Ubuntu, newer interpreters are available from the deadsnakes PPA ( sudo add-apt-repository ppa:deadsnakes/ppa ). It is a genuine convenience, but the maintainers are explicit that timely security updates are not guaranteed . That is fine for a scratch machine and a poor default for production. Prefer uv , pyenv , or building from source when you need a version the distro does not ship. Linux: the per-user route with uv uv installs standalone CPython builds (from the python-build-standalone project) into your home directory. No root, no compilation, no system changes. bash · uv (Astral) copy curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh # review the script first on servers uv python install 3.14 # downloads a standalone build uv python list # available + installed uv python find 3.14 # absolute path to the interpreter uv python pin 3.14 # writes .python-version for this project Piping curl into sh Convenient, and a supply-chain habit worth breaking. For anything you care about, download the script, read it, verify the checksum/signature where the project provides one, then run it. The same applies to installers from any vendor — including Python-adjacent tooling. "It's from a well-known project" is not verification; a compromised release is still a release. Linux: pyenv, when you need exact versions bash · pyenv from source copy # Build dependencies (Debian/Ubuntu) sudo apt install -y make build-essential libssl-dev zlib1g-dev \ libbz2-dev libreadline-dev libsqlite3-dev libffi-dev liblzma-dev \ libncursesw5-dev xz-utils tk-dev libgdbm-dev uuid-dev curl -fsSL https://pyenv.run | bash # then add to ~/.bashrc as printed by the installer exec "$SHELL" -l pyenv install 3.13.7 pyenv versions pyenv global 3.13.7 # default for your user pyenv local 3.12.11 # per-directory override, writes .python-version The classic pyenv failure is a silently missing libsqlite3-dev or libssl-dev : the build succeeds, then import sqlite3 or HTTPS fails. Always run the verification block below after any source build. On Debian/Ubuntu you can alternatively use the maintained python-build-standalone builds that uv and pyenv can consume. Windows: the installer and the Store trap Download the Windows installer from python.org/downloads/windows . Avoid third-party "Python bundles". Tick Add python.exe to PATH on the first screen. If you miss it, re-run the installer and choose Modify rather than reinstalling blindly. Prefer the per-user install unless you have a reason; it avoids UAC-admin surprises with pip. Use the py launcher ( py -0p lists installed versions, py -3.13 -m venv .venv selects one). Bad decision — the Microsoft Store stub named python.exe Windows ships a zero-byte execution alias at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps\python.exe that opens the Store. If it comes first on PATH , running python launches a shop instead of an interpreter, and some tools report "Python was not found". Fix it in Settings → Apps → Advanced app settings → App execution aliases by disabling the python.exe and python3.exe aliases, then ensure your real install's Scripts and root directory precede WindowsApps on PATH . Containers: the reproducibility escape hatch bash · Docker copy docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD":/app -w /app python:3.14-slim bash # inside: python -VV pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt Pin the full image tag or digest ( python:3.14.0-slim-bookworm , or better a @sha256:… digest) for reproducibility. python:latest is a moving target and will break your build on a random Tuesday. Verify the install like you mean it Version output alone proves nothing: a Python can be present but unable to create environments, verify TLS certificates, or import its own standard library modules. CI Matrix, not guesswork Test the oldest version your requires-python allows and the newest stable. A matrix of five versions catches syntax and typing regressions early. Production One pinned minor Pin the exact patch in the image ( 3.13.7-slim ) and rebuild monthly for security patches. Upgrade minors deliberately, not automatically. Bad decision — building with sudo make install Running ./configure && sudo make install overwrites /usr/local/bin/python3 and its stdlib, which sits ahead of the distro's Python on PATH . System tools that expect the distro build can then break in ways that are hard to trace, and uninstalling is genuinely painful (no package record). If you must build from source, use make altinstall and a --prefix inside your home directory, or use pyenv/uv, which do exactly that for you. The five minutes you save are repaid with interest the first time apt misbehaves. This level is the difference between an interpreter you fight and one that behaves. Configuration happens at three scopes: the shell (PATH and exported variables), the interpreter ( site , .pth files, user site), and tooling (pip config, editor, git hooks). Get the order right and everything else composes. 1. PATH: the only config most people need Programs are found through PATH , left to right. Console scripts installed with pip --user and pipx land in ~/.local/bin (Linux/macOS) or %APPDATA%\Python\Python3xx\Scripts (Windows). If that directory is missing from PATH , the install succeeds and the command "does not exist". bash · make user scripts visible (Linux/macOS) copy echo "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | grep -E '\.local/bin|\.venv|pyenv' # Append once, in ~/.profile for POSIX shells, or ~/.zshrc / ~/.bashrc for interactive shells: echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.profile exec "$SHELL" -l command -v pytest ruff uv pipx Which file: .bashrc, .profile, .zshrc? ~/.bashrc runs for interactive non-login shells; ~/.profile runs for login shells (and is read by most display managers); zsh uses ~/.zshrc + ~/.zprofile . GUI applications and systemd services often start without your interactive shell config, so a PATH that works in the terminal can still be missing under systemd. That is why services should call interpreters by absolute path (see Level 13), not rely on PATH . Bad decision — alias python=python3 and alias pip=pip3 It feels harmless. It is not: aliases do not apply to scripts, cron, systemd, IDEs, or subprocess , so you get a machine that behaves one way interactively and another way in production. On Debian/Ubuntu, python is deliberately absent from the base system because Python 2-era tooling would silently pick it up. Worse, alias pip=pip3 hides which interpreter pip belongs to. The robust fix is to create a virtual environment and let python and pip both resolve inside .venv/bin . If you truly need a user-level python , use a symlink in ~/.local/bin pointing at a specific version and understand that every non-shell context will ignore it. 2. pip: configure it once, correctly pip reads configuration from three scopes — global ( /etc/pip.conf ), user ( ~/.config/pip/pip.conf ), and site ( .venv/pip.conf ) — plus PIP_* environment variables. Later scopes win, and command-line flags beat everything. Inspect before editing: bash · pip configuration copy python3 -m pip config debug # every file considered, and its values python3 -m pip config list python3 -m pip --version # confirm which pip, from which environment python3 -m pip cache dir # where wheels are cached ini · ~/.config/pip/pip.conf copy [global] # Only change these if your organisation actually runs a mirror. # index-url = https://pypi.org/simple timeout = 20 retries = 3 disable-pip-version-check = true [install] # Fail loudly instead of silently drifting when a version is yanked. prefer-binary = true Bad decision — trusted-host as a permanent fix Adding trusted-host or --trusted-host disables TLS certificate verification for that index. People add it to silence corporate-proxy errors and then forget it exists; every package they install afterwards is trivially interceptable. The correct fixes are: install your organisation's CA certificate into the system trust store, point pip at it with cert = /path/ca.pem , or configure the proxy in pip.conf . If you inherit a machine with trusted-host set, treat it as a security finding. 3. The environment variables that matter Python honours a set of PYTHON* variables at startup. A few are useful; several are dangerous because they change behaviour for every program you run. Use python -X option or -E / -I in scripts to ignore the environment entirely. Selected PYTHON* environment variables Variable Effect Verdict PYTHONPATH Prepends directories to sys.path . Avoid. Shadowing risk; use installed packages or uv run . PYTHONSTARTUP Script executed by the interactive interpreter only. Safe for conveniences, never for application logic. PYTHONDEVMODE Enables development mode: extra warnings, debug hooks. Good in CI ( PYTHONDEVMODE=1 ). PYTHONWARNINGS Warning filters, e.g. error to turn warnings into exceptions. Useful in tests; do not rely on it in production. PYTHONSAFEPATH Like -P : do not prepend the script's directory / CWD. Good hardening for tools run on untrusted trees. PYTHONNOUSERSITE Ignores

racismo: O Racismo é mais do que Palavras Comparativas Ser "Preto" é ser objectivado e limitado a uma cor só, sem forma, sem irregularidades da cor, tão ou mais escura do que a cor da sombra de um objecto estático ou em movimento ou até, um ser que está parado ou em movimento.
