recycling: Monkey Blog · Second Lives Home EN PT Second lives · a manual in seventeen parts Nothing Is Garbage A bin is a decision someone else already made for you. This manual takes it back: what kitchen scraps, garden clippings, old clothes, jars, tins, pallets and dead electronics can become instead — with the recipes, the numbers, the traps and the sources, for a household, a garden, or a small business. Seventeen parts 75+ second lives Bin audit Compost calculator From waste to income Sources Start with my own bin Part 03: one week, a kitchen scale, and a number instead of a feeling. I want to use the scraps tonight Part 04: five things to do with peels, stale bread and coffee before they become a smell. I have a garden and a compost problem Part 05: the carbon/nitrogen balance, with a calculator that says how many litres to add. I want this to pay Part 13: repair, upcycling, compost and workshops — what people actually charge for. 01 The rule that changes everything Waste is not a property of an object. It is the moment someone stops imagining a use for it. That is good news, because imagination is cheap — and the order in which you apply it decides whether you are solving a problem or just moving it. Refuse — the only free option The bag, the straw, the second plastic tray, the free T-shirt at an event. Every object refused costs nothing to store, sort, clean or feel guilty about. This is the only rung with no downstream work. Reduce — use less of it, for longer A bigger jar of yoghurt, a refill bottle, a repair instead of a replacement. Reduction is boring and it is where most of the kilos actually disappear. Reuse and repair — the interesting middle Jars, crates, clothes, furniture, electronics. This manual lives here: the second life that keeps the material in service without melting it down. Rot — let biology do the work Food scraps and garden clippings are not waste, they are next year's soil. Composting is the cheapest transformation available to a household, and the one most often skipped. Recycle — the last resort that looks like the first Recycling destroys the object to recover the material. It needs energy, clean streams and a market. It is good, and it is fourth best — which is why a page about it should not start there. What you gain Money that stays in the house: a jar, a crate and a repaired lamp are things you no longer buy. Better bins: less smell, fewer flies, no liquid at the bottom, half the volume. Skills that transfer — cutting, sewing, composting, wiring a plug are the same skills at 60 as at 6. A garden that feeds itself instead of importing bags of soil. A reason to know your neighbours: the person with pallets, the café with buckets, the man who fixes toasters. What it costs Time, and the honest admission that ten minutes of labour can be worth less than a €2 object. Storage: the fatal temptation is a garage full of "someday". Every project needs a deadline or it is hoarding with better vocabulary. Standards: some second lives are not safe — food contact, children's toys, electrical work, anything structural. Aesthetic risk: visible mending is beautiful, a shelf made of three different woods is a shelf. The uncomfortable part: recycling is an industry with losses, and much of what you sort is burned or shipped. The scale, in four numbers. The average person in the EU generated 517 kg of municipal waste in 2024, and 48 % of it was recycled or composted. Biowaste is the single largest fraction of that bin at 28.8 % — food and garden waste, the part a household can transform without any industry at all. Globally, 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted in 2022, about 19 % of everything available to consumers, and food loss and waste produce 8–10 % of greenhouse-gas emissions. You cannot compost your way out of a supply chain. You can, however, remove a third of your own bin and half its smell this month. 02 Read the bin: eight materials, eight futures Every object is a material wearing a shape. Identify the material and the options appear — and so do the exclusions, which matter more. What each family wants to become, and where the second life stops being a good idea Family Typical pieces Best second life Where it stops The three questions before you keep anything A house is not a warehouse. Answer all three out loud, because a "maybe" is a no. Do I have a use, today? Not a use in the abstract: this shelf, this window, this person's birthday. Do I have the other half? A jar without a lid, a lamp without a cable, a frame without glass — the missing part is the project. Is it safe for that use? Food, children, heat, electricity and load-bearing are the five things you cannot improvise. 03 Audit your own bin Guilt is a bad measuring instrument. One week, one kitchen scale, five numbers — and you will know exactly which habit is worth changing, instead of changing all of them badly. People in the household Food and garden waste (kg per week) Plastic and metal packaging (kg per week) Paper and cardboard (kg per week) Glass (kg per week) Textiles and other (kg per week) Total / week — Per person / year — Could rot — Could be recycled — Still mixed — How to read the result The EU average is 517 kg per person per year. Under 300 means you are already unusual; over 600 means volume, not guilt, is the place to start. But the number that matters is the third one: the organic share is the only stream a household can process at home, without markets, trucks or a single kilowatt-hour. if organic wins Build the compost, then the garden A balcony bokashi bin handles 15 litres a month and takes no space. A worm bin handles a family's peels, and gives back the only fertiliser you will need for pots. if packaging wins Change the shop, not the bin Packaging is decided at the shelf. Two refill stops, one bigger format and a market with loose produce do more than a year of folding cartons perfectly. if textiles win Open a repair basket A box with needle, thread, patches and a spare button turns "I have nothing to wear" into twenty minutes. The rest becomes rags, then wicks, then compost-adjacent dust. 04 The kitchen: five lives before the bin A kitchen throws away food, water and packaging in the same gesture. These five habits catch the first two, cost nothing, and are the ones people keep doing after the novelty wears off. 20 minutes + 2 weeks · €0 Citrus-peel vinegar cleaner The peels you were going to bin become a degreaser strong enough for the stove. Peels of 3–4 oranges, lemons or limes 1 L of white vinegar (the cheap one) A jar with a lid Pack the peels into the jar and cover with vinegar. Leave it two weeks in a cupboard, shaking when you remember. Strain, keep the liquid, dilute half and half with water for surfaces. Never on marble, limestone or unsealed stone — the acid eats the surface. Never mixed with bleach. 5 minutes · 1–3 weeks Regrow from the end Spring onion, leek, celery, lettuce hearts and carrot tops will push new leaves from a centimetre of water. The root end, 2–3 cm, still attached A shallow glass or a saucer Light, but not direct summer sun Stand the end in 1 cm of water, cut side up. Change the water every day — stagnant water is what rots it. Cut what you need, twice at most, then give the rest to the compost. The second growth is thinner and less flavoured: this is a pleasure, not a food supply. 40 minutes · freezer Scrap stock Onion skins, carrot peel, celery leaves, herb stems, a parmesan rind: a litre of stock from what was already in the bin. A bag of peels kept in the freezer until it is full Cold water to cover, a bay leaf, ten peppercorns Salt, added only at the end Cover the scraps with cold water and bring to a bare simmer. Thirty to forty minutes, never a hard boil — boiling makes it cloudy and bitter. Strain, salt, cool fast, freeze in jars with 2 cm of headspace. No mouldy scraps, no potato leaves or green sprouts (solanine), no cabbage in quantity. Four days in the fridge, three months frozen. 10 minutes · 150 °C Stale bread, three ways Bread does not go off, it goes hard — and hard bread is an ingredient. Croutons: cubes, oil, salt, 15 minutes at 150 °C Pangrattato: blitz with garlic and parsley, toast in a pan Breadcrumbs: blitz dry and freeze in a bag Cut or tear before it turns to stone; a dry loaf grates into crumbs in a minute. Dry it fully before storing, or the bag grows mould. Mould is not a crust problem: the toxins survive toasting. Mouldy bread goes to the compost, never to the oven. 0 minutes · daily Coffee grounds A café gives away kilos of them. They are a green compost input, a mild abrasive and a deodoriser — in that order of usefulness. Compost: a thin layer, never a solid cake — they mat and go anaerobic Scrub: with oil and sugar, for hands and sinks Fridge: a cup in the door absorbs smells for a week Skip the old myth about acid-loving plants: spent grounds are nearly neutral. Do not dump them down the sink. Food safety, in one line each. Cool leftovers fast and shallow. Reheat once. Anything mouldy goes to compost, not to "cut off the bad bit". Rice, pasta and reheated meat are the usual suspects, not the leftovers you can smell. 05 The garden: compost is chemistry with a smell Composting fails for one of three reasons: too wet, too dry, or the wrong balance of carbon to nitrogen. The first two are visible. The third is the one this calculator fixes. Greens, by volume (litres) Browns, by volume (litres) Browns : greens — Add — The target is about 25–30 parts carbon to one part nitrogen, which in practice is two to three volumes of browns for one of greens. Greens are wet and Nitrogen-rich: peels, coffee, grass, fresh leaves. Browns are dry and Carbon-rich: cardboard, egg boxes, dry leaves, straw, sawdust from untreated wood, toilet-roll tubes. fast Hot compost, one cubic metre Build the pile in one go, three parts browns to one of greens, damp as a wrung sponge. It reaches 55–65 °C in three days; turn it when it cools, and it is finished in six to ten weeks. small space Bokashi, on a balcony A sealed bucket with bran inoculated with lactic bacteria ferments everything, including fish and cheese, in two weeks. It is not compost: bury the result 20 cm deep, or feed it to a worm bin. with worms Worm bin, indoors A plastic box, shredded cardboard, a handful of composting worms, and peels buried under the bedding. No smell when it is balanced; citrus, onion and cooked food in quantity upset it. What never goes in a home compost: meat, fish and dairy in an open pile (bokashi is the exception), pet faeces, glossy or thermal paper, treated wood, "compostable" plastic unless your council accepts it, and anything that has been in contact with pesticide. A compost heap is not a furnace: it does not sterilise. The free soil amendments you already own Leaf mould is the slowest and best thing in this section: a wire ring, wet leaves, a year, and you have a seed-sowing compost that costs nothing. Eggshells need crushing and years to break down — they are a slow calcium bank, not a quick fix. Wood ash is potash, useful in small amounts on soil, never on blueberries or acid-lovers, and never from painted or treated wood. 06 Water, used twice A litre that has washed a vegetable is not dirty, it is displaced. The trick is to move it once, by hand or by gravity, and to know what must not go with it. garden Greywater to a mulch basin Bath or shower water, still warm, poured into a shallow basin dug around a tree and covered with wood chips. The soil filters it; the plant drinks it. No tank, no pump, no smell. kitchen Vegetable washing water The bowl you rinsed the lettuce in goes on the houseplants or the balcony pots. One bowl a day is 100 litres a year that never reaches the drain. cooking Pasta, rice and egg water Cooled, unsalted cooking water carries starch that feeds soil life. Salted water goes to the drain, not the pots — a few years of it turns a pot salty. free Air-conditioner condensate A split unit in a Portuguese summer makes litres a day at almost zero conductivity. Perfect for the garden, not for drinking, and not for misting anything you breathe near. Greywater rules that are not negotiable: No kitchen sink water with grease, no dishwasher water, no water from nappies or toilets. No bleach, borax or fabric softener — they kill the soil you are trying to feed. Use it the same day, below the surface, and never on leaves you will eat raw. Not on root vegetables, not on seedlings, not in a drip system that will clog with soap. 07 Textiles: repair first, then remake Clothes are the most emotionally loaded object in the bin. They are also the easiest to keep: a needle, a patch and twenty minutes restore most of what people throw away. Less than 1 % of the material used to make clothes is recycled into new clothes, so the second life you give a shirt is not a small thing. 20 minutes · €0 The repair basket One box by the sofa turns mending from a project into a habit. Needles, two threads (dark and light), small scissors A tin of spare buttons, saved from old shirts Iron-on patches, or denim offcuts for knee repairs Mend while the hole is small: a stitch now, a replacement later. Reinforce the corners of a pocket with a triangle of stitches before they tear. Visible mending is a style, not a confession — sashiko lines look deliberate because they are. 15 minutes · no sewing The T-shirt bag A single shirt becomes a strong, washable bag for the market. One old T-shirt, the thicker the better Scissors Cut off the sleeves and widen the neck into handles. Cut a fringe along the hem, 8 cm deep, front and back. Tie each front fringe to the matching back fringe, two knots, and pull tight. It holds 5 kg of shopping. It does not hold glass bottles without a lining. a weekend · a craft The rag rug Every torn sheet and worn shirt becomes weft. The Portuguese version — trapos — is older than the recycling bin. Old fabric cut into 3 cm strips A hessian sack or a cheap rug base A crochet hook or a prodding tool Work from the centre out, rows 3 cm apart, pushing each strip through and knotting it. Mix colours deliberately: two tones of the same family read as a design. Use cotton and linen; synthetic fleece sheds fibres every wash and does not felt. When a textile is truly finished: cut it into rags first (kitchen, workshop, paint), then use the rags as plant ties or wicks, then take what is left to a textile bank — not the paper bin. Never put textiles in a home compost unless they are pure wool or cotton cut into small pieces; a polyester label will still be there in a decade. 08 Paper and cardboard: the quiet material Cardboard is the most useful free material in a city and the least respected. It is a carbon source for compost, a weed barrier, a seed pot, a firelighter and a prototype — and it is recyclable at the end of all of that. propagation Seed pots from tubes Toilet-roll tubes and newspaper rolls make deep pots for beans, sweet peas and tomatoes, which hate root disturbance. Plant the whole tube: it rots in the soil. weed control Sheet mulch Plain brown cardboard, tape and staples removed, overlapped 15 cm, wetted, covered with 10 cm of wood chips or compost. It smothers grass in a season and feeds worms underneath. fire Fire starters Rolls stuffed with shredded paper and dipped in melted candle ends. One per fire, and the firelighters you stop buying are €3 a box. office Notebooks from misprints Print on one side only and the other side becomes a notebook: fold, staple at the spine, cut the edges. A5 from A4, sixty pages, ten minutes. Paper that must not be composted or mulched: thermal receipts (they are coated and often contain bisphenols), glossy magazines, pizza boxes soaked in grease, anything with plastic tape or laminate, and shredded paper from an office with a confidential-waste contract. Plain brown card, newspaper and office paper are fine. 09 Glass and metal: containers that outlive us Glass is endlessly recyclable and effectively eternal in a cupboard. Metal is the same, with sharper edges. Both reward a little patience and punish improvisation around food and heat. pantry Jars that match their lids A shelf of identical jars with matching lids is better storage than anything you can buy: visible, airtight, stackable. Collect one brand's jars until the lids all fit, then stop collecting. light The jar lantern A clean jar, a length of copper wire as a handle, a candle stub or a solar garden light inside. Twenty minutes, and it is the best-looking thing on a summer table. garden Tin-can planters A large tin, holes punched in the base with a nail, a coat of paint outside: herbs on a wall. Rust is the only maintenance, and herbs do not mind it. protection Bottle cloches The bottom half of a plastic bottle over a seedling is a mini greenhouse for €0. Lift it by day or the plant cooks; the cap off means ventilation. Sharp things, honestly: Cut glass with a proper cutter, oil, and gloves; fire-polish edges or sand them wet. A cut bottle is a blade. Tin cans: file the inside rim, and never use a can that held paint or chemicals for food or for a planter with edible roots. Do not store acidic food in a rusty can or in aluminium that has been cut. Glass is for food; metal is for tools, planters and light. Aerosol cans, gas cartridges and batteries are not craft material. They go to the ecocentro, closed. 10 Wood and furniture: the strong second life Wood is the one material where salvage beats buying on quality, not just on principle. Old pine from a drawer bottom is denser and drier than anything in a DIY shed. structure The pallet bench One pallet, four castors, a cushion: a bench for a balcony in an afternoon. Sand the top, oil it, and check every board for cracks before it takes weight. storage Crates as shelving Wine and fruit crates stack into a shelf that needs no tools, moves with you and can go back to the market. Fix them to the wall if children are in the house. garden Drawers as planters A drawer with holes drilled in the base, lined with cardboard and filled with compost, is a salad bed for a wall or a windowsill. It lasts two or three seasons. repair The wobbly chair Ninety per cent of wobbles are a loose joint: clean the old glue with a knife, warm the joint, add wood glue and clamp for a day. Stronger than new, and free. The wood you must not take: Pallets stamped MB (methyl bromide, a fumigant) — take only HT, heat-treated. The stamp is on the block, not the board. Painted or varnished wood of unknown age: old paint can carry lead. Sanding it is the risk, not keeping it. Railway sleepers, telegraph poles and anything green-tinted from pressure treatment — creosote and arsenic salts do not belong near food or compost. MDF and chipboard that has been wet: it crumbles and the dust is not worth breathing. 11 Electronics: the box you must not open The most valuable waste in your house is also the most dangerous. E-waste contains copper, gold, aluminium and cobalt — and capacitors that hold a lethal charge long after the plug is out. The second life of a device is repair, resale, or a certified recycler. Not a screwdriver and a YouTube video, unless you know which part is which. 62 million tonnes. That is the world's e-waste in 2022, growing five times faster than the recycling that is documented — only about a fifth is formally collected and recycled. A phone in a drawer is not "saved"; it is a mine that has not been opened yet. first Repair before replacement A repair café is the cheapest technician in Europe: volunteers, tools, coffee, and a good chance the toaster only needs a €2 switch.
